source.title: RAZOR: Ratio-Aware Layer Editing for Targeted Unlearning in Vision Transformers and Diffusion Models
source.authors: Ravi Ranjan; Utkarsh Grover; Xiao-Min Lin; Agoritsa Polyzou

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests post-training quantization of unlearned models, reporting residual forget accuracy, in vision and diffusion-model settings rather than the LLM settings in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper applies 8-bit and 4-bit quantization and reports forget accuracy (M1), so those results bear on quantization recovery. It does not test relearning, activation-direction ablation, or prompt-based recovery. It gives no never-trained comparison or stated chance level, so its M1 changes cannot establish how much knowledge was recovered relative to a model that never learned it. Cited claims about prompt recoverability and other attacks are not the paper's own results.
record.test_reason: The study applies 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization to unlearned CLIP models (SSD, LoTUS, SalUn, SLUG, RAZOR). It reports forget accuracy before and after (Table 3), so it bears on D in a vision-language setting, not LLMs. RAZOR's stability under quantization bears on F. No relearning, direction ablation or prompting attacks are run.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors report that quantization degrades unlearning for all methods, with 4-bit worst. Full-model-update methods suffer disproportionately, layer-restricted methods are more robust, and RAZOR stays stable under quantization.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes RAZOR, a ratio-aware vision-model unlearning method, and evaluates post-training quantization; it does not reproduce the cited LLM unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Quantization effects vary by method, bit width, and dataset; the paper reports greater degradation at 4-bit than 8-bit in its general discussion.
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Findings Track (CVPRF); to appear in the proceedings.
record.problems: The quantization table reports means over five random seeds without uncertainty values for these results. No never-trained or pre-unlearning reference, chance level, or direct recovery-to-baseline measure is reported. The experiments are on vision models rather than LLMs.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 M2–M5 values are omitted because the extracted rows focus on forget accuracy, the direct residual-recognition measure for quantization recovery; the other metrics do not directly measure restoration of targeted knowledge.

untested.parts: No attack other than quantization is run; LLM settings are not tested.
No activation-direction ablation or access-vs-deletion analysis.
LLM unlearning methods and recovery relative to pre-unlearning accuracy are not tested; only CLIP is quantized.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
RAZOR's resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits and prompting is not tested, nor its quantization robustness on SD or LLaVA.

record.verdict_notes: Chance level is implied: M1 scores forget images against two prompts [q_forget, q_retain], so about 50% is chance, contrary to the reader's 'no chance stated'. SalUn on CIFAR/ImageNet never forgot (97/88), so those rows cannot show recovery. Table 3 looks unreliable: every quantized M3 is exactly 0.00, and M4/M5 shrink by an almost constant ~0.99 factor. Several rows repeat exactly across datasets: SSD M5 is identical on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; RAZOR M5 and the SSD/LoTUS 4-bit M1 also repeat. These patterns suggest the quantization values were derived rather than measured; treat them with caution. No uncertainty is given for Table 3. LLaVA (Table 6) and Stable Diffusion results involve no recovery attack.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports unlearning and utility metrics and quantizes models, but does not test the full claim that targeted knowledge is brought near chance and remains unrecovered under simple attacks; no chance reference is stated.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack is performed.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis showing access-blocking rather than deletion is performed.
Quantization is tested on vision-model unlearning, not the named LLM unlearning methods. There is no never-trained reference or direct measure of restoration to pre-unlearning performance.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery test is performed.
The paper reports RAZOR's quantization results, but does not test resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits, or prompting attacks, or on LLMs.

tranche.reason: CLIP vision-language unlearning is a new setting. Post-training quantization of the unlearned models gives a result on D.

source_check.notes: Table 3 gives means over five seeds with no spread (the only ± is in the LLaVA table), and it doesn't say which CLIP backbone (ViT-B/32 or ViT-L/14) each row uses. M1 is a two-prompt score, so unlearned values near 50% are near chance, and no pre-unlearning reference is given. SalUn on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet (88-97% at full precision) is left out of the verdicts. D.against[13] files the SLUG/RAZOR result under 'challenges', while this study's verdict l1 is limits_scope. r30 (Table 3: 40.00->40.38) is not in the pack.

statements.correction: RAZOR (authors' own method) on CLIP (OpenCLIP; setup names ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14, Table 3 does not say which). Unnamed 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization. M1 forget accuracy (%): CIFAR-10 52.50->52.99/53.00; ImageNet 53.50->54.00/54.01; LAION-400M 40.00->40.37/40.38 (Table 3). Not an LLM, not WMDP/MUSE. Reviewed (CVPR 2026 Findings), code. Tested against quantization only.
statements.problem: Cites r10, r20, r30 but never names RAZOR or CLIP. Its conditions (7-8B LLMs; WMDP/MUSE; NF4/AWQ/GPTQ/bitsandbytes) and 'why' do not cover this study, so it misplaces the study's evidence.
